passages.t: ‘Blessed is the man who fears the LORD’: the twin of Psalm 111
passages.happening:
Psalm 112 also opens with “Hallelujah!” Then it describes a person. “Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments” (verse 1).

His children will be strong, and his family upright (verse 2). His house is not poor, “and his righteousness endures forever” (verse 3). “Light dawns in the darkness for the upright” (verse 4). He is gracious and compassionate and righteous.

The psalm shows what such a person does. “It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely, whose affairs are guided by justice” (verse 5). He is not knocked down by trouble. “He does not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD” (verse 7). He has given freely: “He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (verse 9).

The last verse looks at the other path. The wicked man sees this and is angry. He grinds his teeth and wastes away, “the desires of the wicked will perish” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Read Psalms 111 and 112 side by side. Both are alphabet poems of the same shape, as the note on Psalm 111 explains. And the words echo. In Psalm 111 God's ‘righteousness endures forever’ (111:3). In Psalm 112 the same is said of the person who fears him (112:3, 9). In 111 the LORD is ‘gracious and compassionate’ (111:4). In 112 the upright person is ‘gracious, compassionate, and righteous’ (112:4). The pair seems to say: the one who fears God comes to look like God.

The opening also echoes Psalm 1: “Blessed is the man” whose “delight is in the Law of the LORD” (Psalm 1:1-2). The book page explains ‘blessed’ (ashre): a whole life going well under God.

In Israel, lending to a poor neighbour was a duty, and the law said no interest was to be charged to the poor. A ‘horn lifted high’ (verse 9) was a picture of honour. ‘Bad news’ (verse 7) meant the kind of report that brought word of war, failed crops or death.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 9 when he asks the church in Corinth to give for the poor: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever” (2 Corinthians 9:9).

Jesus said, “let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). The woman of strength in Proverbs is praised in the same terms as the man here: “She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy” (Proverbs 31:20).
passages.hard: Does verse 3 promise that godly people will always be rich? No. The psalm describes the way God's world tends to work, not a guarantee for every life. Many psalms are the prayers of righteous people who are poor and suffering, and Psalm 73 wrestles openly with the wicked doing well. Notice also what the wealth in Psalm 112 is for: it is lent and given away. Teaching that promises riches in return for faith is not what this psalm says.
passages.asks:
The person in Psalm 112 is not afraid of bad news, because his heart is fixed on God. That steadiness does not come from having no trouble. It comes from trust.

The psalm also asks about money. Is what you have open-handed, like seed scattered on a field? Generosity, in this psalm, is part of what it means to fear the LORD.
